items.caption:
Two short nights turned up hunger in a lab.
In a 2004 University of Chicago study, 12 young men rated hunger 24% higher after two nights of 4 hours in bed than after two of 10 hours. Hormones leptin and ghrelin shifted too. A small lab study.

items.caption:
Your weekend lie-in is a mini jet lag.
In a 2012 Current Biology study of about 65,000 Europeans, a bigger gap between work-day and free-day sleep timing (social jet lag) went with a higher body mass index. An association from questionnaires, not proof of cause.

items.caption:
POV: it's your third snooze.
In one small lab study of 31 regular snoozers, 30 minutes of snoozing cost about 6 minutes of sleep and did not make morning test scores worse (no worse, or slightly better). In a mostly Swedish survey of 1,732 people, 69% said they snooze or set several alarms at least sometimes. Habitual snoozers only, so a clue, not a rule.
